title: Rhombus gardens: duel, fewest blocks and red trapezoids

families.title: Rhombus gardens: duel, fewest blocks and red trapezoids
families.mathematics: Boards are cut from the grid of triangles that pattern blocks fit. In the rhombus duel, players take turns laying a rhombus and a player with no room loses. On a board that looks the same after a half turn, copying wins: when the centre of the turn is a grid point, no rhombus is its own copy, so the second player can always answer with the copy of the last move; when the centre is the middle of an edge, the first player lays the one rhombus across it and copies from then on. Boards without that symmetry are won or lost by search. Fewest blocks: fitting the most hexagons first does not always give the fewest blocks (seven hexagons fit the hexagon of side 3, which then needs 13 blocks, though 12 fill it). A trapezoid covers two up triangles and one down, or two down and one up, so the numbers of each kind are fixed by the board: two-up minus two-down is ups minus downs, and the total is a third of the triangles. Two trapezoids that make a hexagon can be cut three ways, so three re-cuts come back to the start, an odd round trip that rhombus flips can never make.
rules: Pieces cover whole triangles, stay inside the board and never overlap.

puzzles.title: Small hexagon
puzzles.objective: Choose who goes first, then win: take turns laying a rhombus, and whoever has no room on their turn loses.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Choose who goes first, then win.
puzzles.instruction: Choose who goes first, then win: take turns laying a rhombus, and whoever has no room on their turn loses.
puzzles.controls: Me first or You first chooses who starts. Drag across two empty triangles that share a side, or tap them one after the other, to lay your rhombus; I lay mine at once, and it is the light one. After I win, Play again starts over. Undo takes back your last rhombus and my answer.
rules: A rhombus covers two empty triangles that share a side and stays inside the board.
Players take turns. If there is no room for a rhombus on your turn, you lose.
I play every board as well as it can be played.
puzzles.idea: Whatever the first player does, the second can do the same on the opposite side.
puzzles.prerequisites: None once the move is shown. Taking turns.
hints: Play once with you first and once with me first. Who won each time?
Look at where my rhombus goes after yours.
Let me go first. Then lay your rhombus opposite mine.

parent.notice: Whether your child plays at random or starts to answer each rhombus with one opposite it.
parent.prompt: Who won when you went first? When you went second? What did the winner do?
parent.explanation: The hexagon looks the same after a half turn about its middle point. The opposite of any rhombus is free whenever the rhombus was laid, because a rhombus and its opposite never share a triangle when the middle is a grid point. So the second player can always lay the opposite of the first player’s rhombus, and always has a move when the first player did: the first player runs out first. Every game here lasts two or three rhombi.
parent.extension: With real blocks, try the 2-by-2 board (puzzle 3). Does copying still work?
parent.connection: The symmetry strategy (Tweedledum and Tweedledee): a second player who keeps the board symmetric can always move. It wins Cram, the same game with dominoes on a grid of squares, whenever a side is even.

parent.prompt: When you went first and won, where was your first rhombus?
parent.explanation: The strip looks the same after a half turn about the middle of its middle edge. The rhombus across that edge is its own opposite. A first player who lays it leaves two ends that are copies of each other, and then answers each rhombus with its opposite, as the second player does on the small hexagon. parent.connection: When the centre of the half turn is the middle of an edge, one rhombus is its own copy; the first player takes it and becomes the copier.

parent.prompt: How do you know the opposite place is always free?
parent.explanation: The hexagon with sides 2 has a grid point in the middle, so the second player wins by copying. parent.notice: Every one of the 18 first rhombi loses, though there is no copying trick.
parent.prompt: Could you copy here? What goes wrong?
parent.explanation: A half turn takes the triangle to one pointing the other way, so copying is not available. Checking every game shows the second player wins: all 18 first rhombi lose. parent.prompt: How did you find the middle of a board with sides 1, 2 and 3?
parent.explanation: The hexagon with sides 1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3 looks the same after a half turn about its centre, which is the middle of an edge: the centre of a hexagon with sides a, b, c is a grid point exactly when a, b and c are all even or all odd. puzzles.title: The mountain
puzzles.objective: Fill the board with at most 3 blocks.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Fill it with 3 blocks.
puzzles.instruction: Fill the board with at most 3 blocks.
puzzles.controls: Choose a block: triangle, rhombus, trapezoid or hexagon. Drag across its triangles or tap them one after the other; a hexagon can also go down by tapping a yellow dot. Tap a block to lift it, or Clear to lift them all.
rules: Blocks cover whole triangles, stay inside the board and never overlap.
A triangle covers one triangle, a rhombus two, a trapezoid three and a hexagon six.
Solved when every triangle is covered with at most 3 blocks.
puzzles.idea: The hexagon fits, but it leaves three corners that each need a block.
hints: Fill it any way, then count the blocks.
What is left if the hexagon goes in?
Leave the hexagon out: three trapezoids fill it.

parent.notice: Many children start with the hexagon, the biggest block, and end with four.
parent.prompt: You used four with the hexagon. Can you use fewer without it?
parent.explanation: The only hexagon leaves the three corner triangles apart, so it needs three more blocks: four in all. Three trapezoids fill the mountain, in two ways. Two blocks are too few: only a hexagon and a trapezoid together cover nine triangles, and the hexagon forces four. So three is the fewest.
parent.extension: What is the most blocks you can use?  (Nine triangles.)
parent.connection: Greedy choices (the biggest piece first) need not give the best answer.

puzzles.provenance: Week 1 encore K–1 Problem 3 (fewest blocks on the mountain).

puzzles.idea: Each of the six points needs its own block, and no block reaches two points.
hints: Fill it any way, then count the blocks.
Can one block cover two points of the star?
Give each point a block that also reaches into the middle.

parent.notice: The hexagon in the middle leaves six points, so seven blocks.
parent.prompt: How many blocks must the points use, however you fill it?
parent.explanation: No block covers two points of the star, so the six points need six different blocks. Six is enough when each point’s block also takes part of the middle hexagon: six rhombi do it, and so do mixtures of triangles, rhombi and trapezoids (65 ways in all). The hexagon in the middle gives seven.
parent.extension: Find a six-block filling that uses a trapezoid.
parent.connection: A lower bound from pieces that must be different: six points, six blocks.

parent.notice: There is exactly one way with five blocks.
parent.prompt: Which places for the hexagon left room for trapezoids?
parent.explanation: The hexagon fits in three places. Just under the top point, it leaves one triangle at the top and three trapezoids below: five blocks, the only five-block filling. In the other two places the best is six. Without a hexagon, 16 triangles need at least six blocks of at most three.

One hexagon, three trapezoids and one triangle.

parent.notice: Always one hexagon, three trapezoids and one triangle.
parent.prompt: Why can’t two hexagons fit?
parent.explanation: Any two hexagons in the triangle of four overlap, so at most one fits. Without one, 16 triangles need at least six blocks. With one, ten triangles are left, which need at least four blocks of at most three: five in all, and three ways reach it.
parent.extension: Can you do it with the hexagon in the other two places?
parent.connection: The fewest is at least h + ⌈(N − 6h)/3⌉ with h hexagons on N triangles; the best h is not always the most.

parent.notice: The middle hexagon leads to seven; six needs three hexagons.
parent.prompt: With the hexagon in the middle, what is left?
parent.explanation: The middle hexagon leaves a ring of 18 triangles that six trapezoids fill: seven blocks. With one or two hexagons the best is seven too. Three hexagons fit in two ways, each leaving three rhombi: six blocks, and no four hexagons fit.
parent.extension: Why does every possible hexagon cover 2 or 6 of the six middle triangles?
parent.connection: The first move that looks best can rule out the best answer.

puzzles.provenance: Week 1 encore K–1 Problem 6 and grades 2–3 Problem 3 (the hexagon with sides 2).

puzzles.title: Triangle of six
puzzles.objective: Fill the board with at most 9 blocks.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Fill it with 9 blocks.
puzzles.instruction: Fill the board with at most 9 blocks.
puzzles.controls: Choose a block: triangle, rhombus, trapezoid or hexagon. Drag across its triangles or tap them one after the other; a hexagon can also go down by tapping a yellow dot. Tap a block to lift it, or Clear to lift them all.
rules: Blocks cover whole triangles, stay inside the board and never overlap.
A triangle covers one triangle, a rhombus two, a trapezoid three and a hexagon six.
Solved when every triangle is covered with at most 9 blocks.
puzzles.idea: Four hexagons fit, but three give fewer blocks.
hints: How many hexagons can fit at once? How many blocks does that give?
Try one hexagon fewer.
Three hexagons and six trapezoids.

parent.notice: Fitting the most hexagons (four) gives ten blocks; nine needs three.
parent.prompt: With four hexagons in, what shapes are left over?
parent.explanation: Four hexagons fit the triangle of six in only one way, and the twelve triangles left fall apart into pieces that need six more blocks: ten. Three hexagons and six trapezoids fill it with nine, in two ways. Fewer than nine is impossible: the bound h + ⌈(36 − 6h)/3⌉ is 12, 11, 10 and 9 for 0 to 3 hexagons, and four hexagons give ten.
parent.extension: What is the fewest for the triangle of five?
parent.connection: The most of the biggest piece and the fewest pieces are different questions.

puzzles.provenance: New, extending Week 1 encore grades 2–3 Problems 3 and 6 to a larger triangle.

puzzles.title: Hexagon of three
puzzles.objective: Fill the board with at most 12 blocks.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Fill it with 12 blocks.
puzzles.instruction: Fill the board with at most 12 blocks.
puzzles.controls: Choose a block: triangle, rhombus, trapezoid or hexagon. Drag across its triangles or tap them one after the other; a hexagon can also go down by tapping a yellow dot. Tap a block to lift it, or Clear to lift them all.
rules: Blocks cover whole triangles, stay inside the board and never overlap.
A triangle covers one triangle, a rhombus two, a trapezoid three and a hexagon six.
Solved when every triangle is covered with at most 12 blocks.
puzzles.idea: Seven hexagons fit, but the fewest uses six.
hints: How many hexagons can you fit? What is left?
Seven hexagons leave pieces too small for trapezoids.
Six hexagons and six trapezoids.

parent.notice: Seven hexagons fit in two ways and give 13 or 19 blocks.
parent.prompt: After seven hexagons, why can’t trapezoids fill what is left?
parent.explanation: Seven hexagons leave six gaps of two triangles (13 blocks) or twelve single triangles (19). With h hexagons the rest needs at least ⌈(54 − 6h)/3⌉ blocks, so h ≤ 6 gives at least 18 − h, which is 12 at h = 6. Six hexagons and six trapezoids reach 12, in two ways, a sixth of a turn apart.
parent.extension: Can you find both twelve-block fillings?
parent.connection: A bound plus a filling that meets it proves the fewest, the same shape of argument as Rhombus gardens’ dots.

puzzles.provenance: Week 1 encore grades 2–3 Problem 6 and grades 4–5 Problem 10 (the hexagon with sides 3).

puzzles.title: Red arrow
puzzles.objective: Fill the board with trapezoids, or press Can’t if it can’t be done.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Fill it with trapezoids, or press Can’t.
puzzles.instruction: Fill the board with trapezoids, or press Can’t if it can’t be done.
puzzles.controls: Drag across three triangles to lay a trapezoid, or tap them one after the other. Tap a trapezoid to lift it. Clear lifts them all. Press Can’t if no filling exists.
rules: A trapezoid covers three triangles in a row.
Pieces stay inside the board and never overlap.
A trapezoid points up when two of its triangles point up, and down when two point down. The counts above the board show how many of each.
Solved when every triangle is covered, or when you press Can’t and no filling exists.
puzzles.idea: Some shapes can be filled with trapezoids and some cannot.
puzzles.prerequisites: None once the move is shown.
hints: Start at a pointed corner.
A corner triangle has few neighbours. Which trapezoid covers it?
Four trapezoids fill it.

parent.notice: The arrow can be filled, in three ways.
parent.prompt: How did you know where the first trapezoid had to go?
parent.explanation: The arrow has 12 triangles, so four trapezoids could cover it, and they do, in three ways. Each way has two trapezoids pointing up and two pointing down.
parent.extension: Find all three ways.
parent.connection: Fillable or not is the first question about any board; the next puzzles show two ways to be sure it cannot be done.

puzzles.provenance: Week 1 encore K–1 Problem 5 (the arrow, with reds).

puzzles.title: Red ramp
puzzles.objective: Fill the board with trapezoids, or press Can’t if it can’t be done.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Fill it with trapezoids, or press Can’t.
puzzles.instruction: Fill the board with trapezoids, or press Can’t if it can’t be done.
puzzles.controls: Drag across three triangles to lay a trapezoid, or tap them one after the other. Tap a trapezoid to lift it. Clear lifts them all. Press Can’t if no filling exists.
rules: A trapezoid covers three triangles in a row.
Pieces stay inside the board and never overlap.
A trapezoid points up when two of its triangles point up, and down when two point down. The counts above the board show how many of each.
Solved when every triangle is covered, or when you press Can’t and no filling exists.
puzzles.idea: A board that rhombi cannot fill can still take trapezoids.
hints: Start at the narrow end.
Look along the bottom row.
Five trapezoids fill it.

parent.notice: Five trapezoids fill it, in five ways; rhombi never can.
parent.prompt: Could rhombi fill this ramp? Count the triangles pointing up and pointing down.
parent.explanation: The ramp has 15 triangles, nine pointing up and six down. Five trapezoids fill it, and every filling has four pointing up and one pointing down. Rhombi cannot: each covers one up and one down, and the counts differ.
parent.extension: How many trapezoids point down in each of the five ways?
parent.connection: Counting ups and downs settles questions for rhombi and, as puzzle 8 shows, for trapezoids too.

puzzles.provenance: Week 1 encore K–1 Problem 5 (the trapezoid board: five reds, and no blues).

puzzles.title: Red hexagon
puzzles.objective: Fill the board with trapezoids, or press Can’t if it can’t be done.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Fill it with trapezoids, or press Can’t.
puzzles.instruction: Fill the board with trapezoids, or press Can’t if it can’t be done.
puzzles.controls: Drag across three triangles to lay a trapezoid, or tap them one after the other. Tap a trapezoid to lift it. Clear lifts them all. Press Can’t if no filling exists.
rules: A trapezoid covers three triangles in a row.
Pieces stay inside the board and never overlap.
A trapezoid points up when two of its triangles point up, and down when two point down. The counts above the board show how many of each.
Solved when every triangle is covered, or when you press Can’t and no filling exists.
puzzles.idea: A count can prove a filling impossible.
hints: Fill as much as you can. Is a triangle always left over?
Count the triangles. Each trapezoid covers three.
Sixteen is not a number of threes. Press Can’t.

parent.notice: Every try leaves one triangle over.
parent.prompt: How many triangles are there? Can trapezoids of three make that many?
parent.explanation: The hexagon has 16 triangles. Trapezoids cover three each, so any filling covers a multiple of three triangles, and 16 is not one. No filling exists, whatever the shape. (Eight rhombi fill it, in six ways.)
parent.extension: Which board on this page could you change by one triangle so that trapezoids fit?
parent.connection: An invariant: the number of triangles covered is always a multiple of three.

puzzles.provenance: Week 1 encore K–1 Problem 5 (the hexagon 2, 1, 2: reds X).

puzzles.title: Two ways
puzzles.objective: Find every way to fill the board with trapezoids, then press That’s all.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Find every way to fill it.
puzzles.instruction: Find every way to fill the board with trapezoids, then press That’s all.
puzzles.controls: Drag across three triangles to lay a trapezoid, or tap them one after the other. Tap a trapezoid to lift it. Each way you fill the board joins the row below. Clear lifts every trapezoid. Press That’s all when you have every way.
rules: A trapezoid covers three triangles in a row.
Pieces stay inside the board and never overlap.
A trapezoid points up when two of its triangles point up, and down when two point down. The counts above the board show how many of each.
Two ways are different when any trapezoid lies in a different place. The board never turns.
Solved when you press That’s all with every way found.
puzzles.idea: The mountain takes trapezoids in two ways, mirror images.
hints: Fill it, then press Clear and fill it another way.
Look at the top corner. Which trapezoids can cover it?
There are two ways, mirror images of each other.

parent.notice: Both ways have three trapezoids pointing up and none down.
parent.prompt: How do you know there isn’t a third way?
parent.explanation: The top triangle is covered by a trapezoid running down the left side or the right side; either choice fills the rest one way. So there are two fillings, mirror images. Each has three trapezoids pointing up: the mountain has six up triangles and three down, so every trapezoid must take two ups.
parent.extension: Why must every trapezoid here point up?
parent.connection: With two ups for every down, no trapezoid can take two downs.

puzzles.provenance: Week 1 encore grades 2–3 Problem 4 (the triangle board: every red filling).

puzzles.title: Nine ways
puzzles.objective: Find every way to fill the board with trapezoids, then press That’s all.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Find every way to fill it.
puzzles.instruction: Find every way to fill the board with trapezoids, then press That’s all.
puzzles.controls: Drag across three triangles to lay a trapezoid, or tap them one after the other. Tap a trapezoid to lift it. Each way you fill the board joins the row below. Clear lifts every trapezoid. Press That’s all when you have every way.
rules: A trapezoid covers three triangles in a row.
Pieces stay inside the board and never overlap.
A trapezoid points up when two of its triangles point up, and down when two point down. The counts above the board show how many of each.
Two ways are different when any trapezoid lies in a different place. The board never turns.
Solved when you press That’s all with every way found.
puzzles.idea: An outer ring and a middle: three rings times three ways to cut the middle.
puzzles.prerequisites: Keeping track of a list. Puzzle 4.
hints: Fill it, then press Clear and find another.
Is the middle hexagon always made of two trapezoids?
The ring round the middle can go three ways, and the middle can be cut three ways.

parent.notice: Every filling has four trapezoids pointing up and four pointing down.
parent.prompt: How can you be sure you have them all?
parent.explanation: The six triangles round the middle point always end up as two trapezoids making a hexagon, which can be cut three ways. The ring of 18 triangles outside it can be filled three ways (two pinwheels turning opposite ways, and one frame). Three times three is nine. Turned or flipped copies count as different here; up to turning there are three, one per ring.
parent.extension: Why does every filling have four of each kind? (Twelve ups and twelve downs.)
parent.connection: Counting by cases: a structure (ring and middle) turns a list into a product.

puzzles.provenance: Week 1 encore grades 2–3 Problem 4 and grades 4–5 Problem 7 (every red filling of the hexagon with sides 2).

puzzles.title: Odd way home
puzzles.objective: Change the filling and come back to ⚑ after an odd number of moves. A move picks up two trapezoids and lays them back a different way.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Come back to ⚑ in an odd number of moves.
puzzles.instruction: Change the filling and come back to ⚑ after an odd number of moves. A move picks up two trapezoids and lays them back a different way.
puzzles.controls: Tap a trapezoid, then another that makes a hexagon with it, to cut that hexagon the next way round. Start again goes back to ⚑.
rules: A trapezoid covers three triangles in a row.
Pieces stay inside the board and never overlap.
A trapezoid points up when two of its triangles point up, and down when two point down. The counts above the board show how many of each.
Two trapezoids that make a hexagon can be cut three ways. A move re-cuts one such hexagon.
Solved when the board matches ⚑ again after an odd number of moves.
puzzles.idea: Two trapezoids that make a hexagon can be cut three ways, so three moves come back.
puzzles.prerequisites: Puzzle 5 helps. Telling odd from even.
hints: Tap two trapezoids that fit together to re-cut them.
Which two trapezoids make a hexagon?
Re-cut the middle hexagon three times.

parent.notice: Only the two trapezoids in the middle can be re-cut on this board.
parent.prompt: Rhombus flips can never come back in an odd number. Why can trapezoids?
parent.explanation: A move picks up two trapezoids and lays them back a different way. Two trapezoids that make a hexagon can be cut three ways, so cutting the middle hexagon three times returns to the start: three moves, an odd number. Rhombus fillings cannot do this: each flip adds or takes away one cube, so a way back has as many of each and is even (Proofs, the flip-map puzzles).
parent.extension: Can the outer ring ever change by moves of two trapezoids? (No: no two ring trapezoids make a hexagon.)
parent.connection: An odd cycle in the move graph; the rhombus flip graph has none because it is bipartite.

puzzles.provenance: Week 1 encore grades 4–5 Problem 8 (moves that pick up two trapezoids; an odd way back).

puzzles.title: Three pointing down
puzzles.objective: Fill the board with trapezoids so that 3 of them point down, or press Can’t if it can’t be done.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Make 3 point down, or press Can’t.
puzzles.instruction: Fill the board with trapezoids so that 3 of them point down, or press Can’t if it can’t be done.
puzzles.controls: Drag across three triangles to lay a trapezoid, or tap them one after the other. Tap a trapezoid to lift it. Clear lifts them all. Press Can’t if no filling has that many pointing down.
rules: A trapezoid covers three triangles in a row.
Pieces stay inside the board and never overlap.
A trapezoid points up when two of its triangles point up, and down when two point down. The counts above the board show how many of each.
Solved when every triangle is covered with 3 pointing down, or when you press Can’t and no filling does that.
puzzles.idea: Fill a big triangle and count how many trapezoids point down.
hints: Fill the triangle any way, and watch the counts above it.
Change a few trapezoids. Do the counts change?
Any filling has three pointing down.

parent.notice: However the triangle is filled, three trapezoids point down.
parent.prompt: Did the number pointing down ever change?
parent.explanation: Any filling works: all 220 fillings of the triangle of six have three trapezoids pointing down and nine pointing up. Puzzle 8 asks why.
parent.extension: Try to make four point down.
parent.connection: The first sight of an invariant: a number that stays the same however the board is filled.

puzzles.provenance: Week 1 encore grades 2–3 Problem 7 (the triangle with six edges on a side: the most two-down reds).

puzzles.title: Four pointing down
puzzles.objective: Fill the board with trapezoids so that 4 of them point down, or press Can’t if it can’t be done.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Make 4 point down, or press Can’t.
puzzles.instruction: Fill the board with trapezoids so that 4 of them point down, or press Can’t if it can’t be done.
puzzles.controls: Drag across three triangles to lay a trapezoid, or tap them one after the other. Tap a trapezoid to lift it. Clear lifts them all. Press Can’t if no filling has that many pointing down.
rules: A trapezoid covers three triangles in a row.
Pieces stay inside the board and never overlap.
A trapezoid points up when two of its triangles point up, and down when two point down. The counts above the board show how many of each.
Solved when every triangle is covered with 4 pointing down, or when you press Can’t and no filling does that.
puzzles.idea: Ups and downs fix how many trapezoids of each kind every filling uses.
hints: Try to fill it with four pointing down.
Count the triangles pointing up and pointing down: 21 and 15.
Each trapezoid pointing up takes one more up than down. Press Can’t.

parent.notice: Every filling has exactly three pointing down, so four is impossible.
parent.prompt: Each trapezoid pointing up uses one more up triangle than down. How many more ups than downs does the whole triangle have?
parent.explanation: The triangle of six has 21 triangles pointing up and 15 down. A trapezoid pointing up covers one more up than down; one pointing down covers one more down than up. So (pointing up) − (pointing down) = 21 − 15 = 6, and (pointing up) + (pointing down) = 36 ÷ 3 = 12. That makes nine up and three down in every filling, so four down is impossible.
parent.extension: For a triangle with 3k edges on a side, how many trapezoids point down?
parent.connection: An invariant from weights: count each up triangle +1 and each down triangle −1. A trapezoid weighs +1 or −1 by its kind, and the board weighs 6, whatever the filling.

puzzles.provenance: Week 1 encore grades 2–3 Problem 7, posed as the review card asks: “fill triangle 6 with 4 two-down” is impossible.
